title: Reading the rings in a roof
bodyMd:
A tree adds a ring of new wood in every growing season, and the width of that ring records the conditions of the year: broad after a mild, wet summer, narrow after a drought or a late frost. Trees of the same species growing in the same region meet the same weather, so their ring widths rise and fall together, and a long run of rings works rather like a bar code. Dendrochronology, the dating of wood by its rings, rests on this. A reference sequence is built by overlapping the patterns of many timbers whose dates are already known. A sample from a beam of unknown age is then slid along the sequence, and if its pattern fits at one position only, each of its rings can be given a calendar year. Simply counting the rings would give the age of the tree, not the year in which it grew.

A dated beam does not, however, date a building. The rings tell us the years in which the tree grew, and they give the year of felling only if the outermost ring survives, just under the bark. Timber was often squared with an axe, and a squared beam has usually lost its outer rings. In that case the last surviving ring gives only a year before which the tree cannot have been felled, and researchers add an allowance for the missing sapwood, which produces a range of years instead of a single one.

Consider the roof of the abbey of San Lorenzo in Valdera. The team sampled twenty-four beams, of which nineteen could be dated. Fourteen had kept their outermost ring, and all fourteen had been felled between 1446 and 1448. The other five had been squared, and their last surviving rings dated from 1431 to 1444. Two of the nineteen carried the marks of joints that fit nothing in the present frame. The abbey's records had implied that the roof was replaced gradually over a century; the pattern of dates suggested instead that most of its timber was cut in a single campaign. Even so, the researchers declined to announce a date for the roof. A beam reused from an older building would still give its original felling date, so the two marked beams, whatever their dates, could not be taken as evidence of when the frame was put together.
accessibilityText: A three-paragraph scientific passage of about 340 words on dating timber by its growth rings. The first paragraph explains that each ring records the weather of one year, that trees of the same species in the same region share a pattern of broad and narrow rings, and that a sample of unknown age can be given calendar years if its pattern fits a reference sequence built from timbers of known date at one position only; counting rings alone gives the tree's age, not the year it grew. The second paragraph says a dated beam does not date a building: rings give the year of felling only if the outermost ring survives, and a beam squared with an axe has usually lost its outer rings, so researchers add an allowance for missing sapwood and give a range of years. The third paragraph describes the roof of the abbey of San Lorenzo in Valdera: twenty-four beams were sampled and nineteen could be dated; fourteen kept their outermost ring and were all felled between 1446 and 1448; five had been squared and their last surviving rings dated from 1431 to 1444; two of the nineteen carried marks of joints that fit nothing in the present frame. The abbey's records implied gradual replacement over a century, while the dates suggested a single campaign of cutting, but the researchers declined to date the roof because a reused beam would still give its original felling date.

provenance.notes: Original prose written for this question bank. The abbey, the beams and every date and count in the third paragraph are invented. The first two paragraphs state the standard textbook principles of tree-ring dating in general terms. No published text was copied, paraphrased or reconstructed, and no author is quoted.
